📌 Tehran, IRNA — Long a man of the military with political aspirations in peacetime, Iran’s security chief now finds himself at the center of wartime defense, with a chance to accomplish a longtime goal.

On June 17, 2025, as Israel was waging war on Iran, Mohsen Rezaei appeared on state TV in his IRGC fatigues and humbly asked that Iran’s then-Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei assign him to a more hands-on role in Iran’s defense.
​
“I ask the Leader of the Revolution to give me, too, a role in the field so that I can be on the frontline together with my brothers-in-arms,” said Rezaei, a veteran of the Iran-Iraq war and a former chief commander of the IRGC (Islamic Revolution Guards Corps) who at the time held membership in Iran’s Expediency Council.
​
It was Iran’s next leader, Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei, who granted that request. Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei, who was elected leader on March 8 following the martyrdom of his father in US-Israeli airstrikes, appointed Rezaei his representative to the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) on August 9, and on the same day, President Masoud Pezeshkian appointed Rezaei secretary of the SNSC. Rezaei was thereby anointed Iran’s security chief.
​
The 12-day Israeli war on Iran, joined briefly by the U.S., was the first shooting war that Iran faced since Rezaei’s days as IRGC commander, including during the Iraqi invasion of Iran in the 1980s. In the decades since he gave up that job in 1997, and before the Israeli war in June 2025, Rezaei attempted several forays into politics in the form of unsuccessful presidential campaigns, in which he often held himself up as the person with the credentials to fix the Iranian economy, reeling from mismanagement and U.S.-spearheaded sanctions.

Then, Israel used its leverage with U.S. President Donald Trump — believed to have been obtained via a global blackmail snare laid by convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein — to draw America all the way in. Together, Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran in February 2026. Just over five months later, Rezaei was put in charge of Iran’s defense.
​
While he has kept up a tradition of refusing to capitulate militarily or diplomatically, he seems to be setting his sights higher. If it truly is his moment, Rezaei seems willing to seize it.
​
By his own admission, opposed to previous rounds of negotiations with the U.S., Rezaei knows that, with intransigent enemies armed to the teeth, one speaks best the language of force. In a war on Iran’s home front, what better way to drive that point home than to make the enemies feel it on theirs?

Trump’s $1.5 Trillion Pentagon Gamble Hits a Political Wall 🏛

Trump’s push to dramatically expand America’s military budget is running into a growing problem in Washington: even some Republicans are struggling to agree on how to pay for it, while Democrats are demanding greater accountability for the administration’s war spending.

The White House is seeking a record $1.5 trillion for defense in fiscal year 2027, a proposal that would mark a major increase in military spending. But the plan is facing mounting resistance as lawmakers debate its cost, its priorities and the administration’s handling of the conflict with Iran.

The proposal combines conventional military investments with some of Trump’s signature ambitions, including a next-generation missile defense system known as the Golden Dome, a new generation of warships and advanced fighter aircraft. The administration has also floated the idea of renaming the Defense Department the Department of War.

The scale of the request is only part of the problem. The administration has divided the proposed funding into two tracks: roughly $1.15 trillion that would require at least some Democratic support and another $350 billion intended to move through a party-line budget process. Republicans have yet to reach agreement on how to advance the latter package, exposing divisions within the president’s own party.

Democrats say they are reluctant to approve additional funding for the Iran war without stronger oversight and clear answers about the administration’s objectives. 

Republicans counter that delaying defense legislation could weaken military readiness at a time when American forces are operating under growing pressure. The dispute is unfolding amid strained relations between Congress and Defense Secretary Hegseth. 

Lawmakers from both parties have expressed frustration over restricted briefings, confrontational exchanges and what they describe as a breakdown in the trust traditionally needed to pass major defense legislation.The war itself is adding urgency to the debate. According to figures cited in reporting by one high-ranking official, the conflict with Iran has cost the United States more than $47 billion. 

The fighting has also placed additional demands on weapons stockpiles, while military training and maintenance have faced delays. For defense planners, replenishing depleted inventories is a pressing concern. 

For lawmakers, however, the question is whether the administration’s proposed spending package adequately distinguishes immediate military needs from expensive projects tied to the president’s broader vision.

The political calendar makes the challenge harder. With another election approaching and Democrats potentially preparing for more aggressive congressional oversight, negotiations over the budget are becoming entangled with wider battles over war policy, executive power and fiscal priorities.

The annual defense authorization bill is also stalled, raising doubts about whether Congress can approve the full package before the end of the year. Trump’s proposal is therefore about more than military hardware. 

It has become a test of whether the administration can turn its ambitions into legislation, persuade skeptical lawmakers and maintain support for an increasingly costly war. 

For now, the $1.5 trillion plan remains a request, not an approved budget, and its final shape will depend on negotiations on Capitol Hill.
